installation.note: chown is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: chown (change owner) modifies the ownership of files and directories. It changes both the user owner and optionally the group owner. Essential for managing file access when files need to belong to different users or groups, especially in multi-user systems or when setting up services.

syntax.description: Change ownership of FILE(s) to OWNER. Optionally specify GROUP with OWNER:GROUP. Requires appropriate permissions (usually root or file owner).

misconceptions.title: chown works without sudo
misconceptions.misconception: Any user can change file ownership
misconceptions.reality: chown requires root/sudo privileges, unless you're the current owner changing to yourself. Regular users cannot change ownership to other users.
misconceptions.tip: Use sudo chown for ownership changes. Only root can change ownership to other users.

misconceptions.title: chown and chmod are the same
misconceptions.misconception: chown and chmod do the same thing
misconceptions.reality: chown changes ownership (who owns the file), chmod changes permissions (what can be done with the file). They're related but different.
misconceptions.tip: chown = ownership (user/group), chmod = permissions (read/write/execute). Use both for complete file access control.

common_pitfalls.solution: Use sudo chown for ownership changes. Only root can change ownership to other users.

common_pitfalls.description: Recursively changing ownership of entire system
common_pitfalls.solution: Be very careful with chown -R. Double-check the path. Never run chown -R / (would change entire system).

common_pitfalls.description: Typo in username or group name
common_pitfalls.solution: Verify user/group exists: id username, getent group groupname. chown will fail if user/group doesn't exist.

best_practices: Use sudo chown for ownership changes
Use chown user:group format for both owner and group
Use chown -R carefully - verify path before running
Verify ownership with ls -l after chown
Use :group to change only group without changing owner
Common pattern: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www for web servers
Never run chown -R / (would change entire system ownership)
performance_tips: chown -R can be slow on large directory trees
Use -v to see progress on recursive operations

additional_notes.permissions: chown requires root/sudo privileges (unless changing to yourself)
additional_notes.format: Format: chown user:group file (both), chown user file (owner only), chown :group file (group only)
additional_notes.vs_chmod: chown = ownership (who owns), chmod = permissions (what can be done). Use both for access control.
additional_notes.common_use: Very common: sudo chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www (web servers), sudo chown user:group service-files (services)
additional_notes.verification: Use ls -l to verify ownership. Third column = owner, fourth column = group.
